Roberts's flat-headed bat (Sauromys petrophilus) is a small molossid endemic to southern Africa, where it occupies rock crevices in arid and semi-arid regions. Field records indicate that neonatal individuals weigh approximately 5.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.4 grams] at birth, a modest mass typical of altricial molossid pups. This low birth weight, compared to the ultimate wet weight for females of 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams], suggests an extended period of maternal investment during the suckling juvenile stage. The species exhibits a slow life-history pace relative to other insectivorous bats of similar size, with females producing only a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. This maximum reproductive rate is remarkably constrained and contributes to low annual recruitment. The timing of these life events appears to be closely linked to ambient thermal conditions, as many physiological processes in this crevice-dwelling species are temperature-dependent.

The gestation period in S. petrophilus is comparatively lengthy for a bat of its body mass, with females carrying the developing foetus for 175 days [tg = 175 days] when maintained under the stable thermal conditions of deep rock crevices, which approximate 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This extended embryogenesis, exceeding the gestation duration reported for several larger molossids, may reflect the energetic constraints of a single-offspring reproductive strategy in a thermally buffered but resource-limited environment. Following parturition, the altricial neonate undergoes a period of rapid mass gain while nursing, relying entirely on the mother's milk before transitioning to solid food. The time since birth at weaning, marking the onset of nutritional independence, is observed at 45 days [tx = 45 days] under these same conditions at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. At this stage, the young bat begins to forage independently, although its body mass remains well below the asymptotic adult female mass, indicating a considerable growth trajectory still ahead.

Sexual maturation in Sauromys petrophilus occurs considerably later, underscoring the species' adherence to a slow life-history strategy. Puberty, defined by the initiation of gametogenesis, is typically reached at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] when measured at the warmer temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], which represents the active metabolic body temperature of this species during flight. This one-year delay to reproductive maturity is a notable feature among molossids, many of which can breed within their first year. The prolonged juvenile phase allows for the completion of somatic growth and the acquisition of foraging skills in the challenging arid environment. During this sub-adult period, individuals continue to gain mass, eventually approaching the ultimate female wet weight of 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams], a figure that can vary between 9 and 22 grams depending on local resource availability and seasonal conditions.

Longevity data for S. petrophilus, derived from field recapture studies and comparisons with the closely related species Eumops perotis, suggest a maximum lifespan of 20 years [am = 20 years] under the stable thermal conditions of rock crevices at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This remarkable lifespan, exceeding that of many similarly sized mammals, is consistent with the species' low reproductive output and delayed maturation, forming a classic slow life-history continuum. Such extended survival places significant selective pressure on the maintenance of physiological homeostasis over many years. The basal metabolic rate of this species has been measured under controlled laboratory conditions, providing insight into the energetic costs of this long-lived lifestyle. Resting metabolic rate assessments reveal a modest daily energetic demand, reflecting the energy-conserving behavior typical of crevice-dwelling bats that rely on torpor to cope with unpredictable food supplies in their semi-arid habitat.

Physiological measurements of Sauromys petrophilus confirm its low metabolic expenditure, a trait shared with other rock-dwelling molossids. Respirometry trials conducted at the species' typical active body temperature recorded a resting metabolic rate of 6.74 milliliters per hour [JOi = 6.74 milliliters per hour] when measured at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This basal oxygen consumption rate is notably low for a mammal of its size, aligning with the energy-conserving strategy expected in an arid-zone insectivore. The pronounced difference between the thermal conditions of rest and activity is ecologically significant; while roosting at ambient crevice temperatures of around 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the bat experiences a moderate metabolic rate, whereas during flight, body temperature rises to 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], elevating metabolic output considerably. This thermal flexibility is key to its survival, allowing the species to buffer against both nocturnal cold and diurnal heat while maintaining a long maximum lifespan of two decades [am = two decades] in the rugged landscapes of southern Africa.
